Senses.Explanation: To throw a brick to draw out jade is to offer something deliberately lesser in hopes of eliciting something finer. Hanxiu Ruqian and Langting Jingting retell Zhaozhou inviting questions as throwing a brick, only to draw out another clod. Shending Yikui praises an official's attempt to elicit jade but says he still missed his household treasure. Zhufeng Zhenxu applies the image to Shakyamuni eliciting Mahakasyapa, while Tianyin Yuanxiu accepts a layman's letter as a successful brick that reveals his capacity. Chan deployment therefore tests both halves of the tactic: what bait is offered and whether the response is actually jade.

Senses.Explanation: One instruction says that in traveling on foot and dwelling in the world one must first “establish firm footing, not be stirred by the eight winds” (立定腳跟，不被八風所鼓). A verse places it as a rock amid vast waves; a public exchange receives the direct interjection, “establish firm footing well” (立定腳跟好). The corpus also corrects a rigid use of the phrase: Zhean Jingfan says that always establishing firm footing can, upon close examination, be “a one-sided, withered understanding and a dull fellow who does not comprehend adaptation” (偏枯見解、不達權變之笨漢). Zen therefore bends bodily footing into a recurrent instruction and appraisal for remaining steady, while preserving a recorded warning that immobility itself can be faulted.

Senses.Note: One independent allowlisted source in the researched concordance clearly anchors this physical referent, so the sense remains provisional. It is placed second because the Zen-loaded figurative sense is primary in this corpus.

Senses.Explanation: “Where you stand is all genuine” is paired with acting as host wherever one is, then repeated as a Fayan-house characterization and as a predicate of immediate use. Literally, at the place of standing or taking one's position , all is genuine or real : "where you stand is all genuine." It occurs 35 times in 24 allowlisted texts. Linji's record supplies the governing formula twice: "act as host wherever you are; where you stand is all genuine; arriving circumstances cannot turn you around" . The second passage precedes it with "do not receive another person's delusion" and follows it by warning that a single doubtful thought gives an opening. Jingtu Huimin reverses its paired order as "where you stand is all genuine; act as host according to the place" . Zhongyan Huayan Zujue attaches it to "take it up and immediately use it" , while Zhenjing Kewen explicitly quotes Linji's wording as "bring it and immediately use it; where you stand is all genuine" . Chan bends the ordinary idea of a standing-place into a stable Linji roster phrase about taking the host position amid changing circumstances; the entry reports the formula and its transmitted predicates without adding a claim beyond those recorded predicates.

Senses.Explanation: Standing in the snow primarily recalls Huike’s vigil before Bodhidharma; a separate image compares a white heron standing in snow. Huike's vigil in the snow before Bodhidharma. Huike, still called Shenguang in the account, stands unmoving through a night of heavy snow until it rises above his knees, and Bodhidharma asks, “You have stood long in the snow; what do you seek?” (汝久立雪中，當求何事). Retrospective formulas join “standing in the snow” with “cutting off the arm” (立雪斷臂), transmission of the robe and bowl, and Huike's request for the buddhas' essential way. Later masters preserve conflicting appraisals: Shuwei Tongxuan says, “standing in snow was not yet toil; cutting off the arm was the real thing,” while Bailu Xianduan calls “the Second Patriarch standing in snow to seek mind” unworthy. It also becomes a stock public question—“what is the meaning of the Second Patriarch standing waist-deep in snow?”—to which Jiangshan Faquan answers, “a leap month comes once in three years.” The ordinary weather action has thus become the compact name of a lineage encounter and a recurring interview prompt.

Senses.Note: The heron forms (鷺鶿 and 鷺鷥) are graphic variants within one physical-action family. The direct answer and the verse comparison are different deployments of the same bird-and-snow scene, not further senses.

Zisheng Shengqin answers a question about proceeding within the four deportments with “a heron stands in the snow” (鷺鶿立雪). To request instruction is to approach an instructor for an answer, clarification, or further examination. The Blue Cliff Record uses the term as a named question-type and distinguishes a long-standing student's request after seeing but not penetrating or penetrating but not clarifying. Other records use it for a first announced request, an attendant's follow-up after an exchange, and biographical visits to an instructor. These are deployments of the same act of asking to receive further explanation; noun and verb grammar do not make separate senses.
Senses.Note: The frozen corpus has 1,949 exact hits in 314 files representing 310 works. Eight anchors cover direct requests, narrated teacher-student visits, follow-up questioning, and explicit classification of the request-for-instruction question across independent works.

Occurrences.Kwic: 沒先聖。且道說箇甚麼？師乃拂袖下去。穴擲下拄杖，歸方丈。侍者隨後請益曰：念法華因甚不祇對和尚？穴曰：念法華會也。次日，師與真
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Strict Lineage of the Five Lamps (五燈嚴統(第10卷-第25卷)), in the Shoushan Xingnian biography: an unnamed attendant is the exact questioner seeking clarification from Fengxue Yanzhao about why Shoushan did not answer him; Fengxue responds that Shoushan understood. The line, expanded context, section header, book title, TEI header, and parallel-passage search leave the attendant unnamed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 打云：「蒼天蒼天！」一僧進方丈，纔展具，師便喝，僧云：「特來請益和尚！」師驀面一掌，僧云：「痛快痛快！」師復打，僧擬進語，師
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Sanshan Lai (三山來禪師語錄): an unnamed monk tells Sanshan Denglai that he has come especially to request instruction. The line, expanded context, section header, book title, TEI header, and parallel search leave the monk unnamed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 古禪師郡之江氏子，少列黌序。初參萬松於華嚴，三載始薙髮。請益於松，松示偈曰：閃灼電光寒，忻然出寶匣。曠劫無明根，一時都抹
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Orthodox Continuation of the Lamp (續燈正統): the compiler narrates Yun’an Denggu requesting further instruction from Wansong Xingxiu; the wording is biography, not either participant’s utterance.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: The biography says 雲菴登古禪師…請益於松: its compiler narrates Yunan Denggu's request to Wansong Xingxiu; neither participant speaks this clause.

Occurrences.Kwic: 但覺心境對立，與古人「天地同根，萬物一體」語不能契合，因請益於龍池，龍池云：「汝若到這田地，便乃放身倒臥，更無別語。」後屢請益，惟遭罵詈
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Miyun (密雲禪師語錄): the compiler narrates Miyun Yuanwu requesting further instruction from Longchi Huanyou; the line is biography rather than Miyun’s utterance.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: The biographical sequence says 因請益於龍池 and 後屢請益 about Miyun Yuanwu's approaches to Longchi Huanyou; it is not direct speech by either master.
